title: A tool for sprite frames derived from pixels we already ship
tier_reason: The derived-art lane already carries real shipped assets (bot_mk2, neighbour, the worm body, the sprinkler idle) but has no tool, so every one of them was a throwaway script.
ask:
Build tools/spritesmith.py: a small library for authoring sprite frames out of pixels already in assets/sprites/, with no model call.

Why: a growing share of shipped art is derived rather than generated (see CREDITS.md — bot_mk2 is a hue rotation of bot, neighbour is a palette remap of characters, the worm body is one repeated cross-section, the sprinkler idle is its spraying frame minus droplets, the rabbit's eyes were restored by hand after downscaling). Each was written as a one-off script and thrown away. Derived frames cannot drift from their source, introduce no new palette entries, and cost nothing, so this lane should be a tool rather than an improvisation.

Required operations, all preserving the pipeline's invariants (colours snapped to the union of the shipped sheets' palettes, alpha strictly 0 or 255, cells aligned to the sheet's grid):
- pivot rotation: rotate a sprite about a named pixel with nearest-neighbour sampling, then snap back to the source palette (a tool swung about the butt of its handle)
- palette remap: map one ramp onto another by name, the neighbour.png operation
- cell compose: assemble frames into a sheet in a named layout, and mirror a row
- depth compose: paste a held object behind or in front of a body per frame
- verify: assert a finished sheet adds no colour absent from the shipped sheets and no partial alpha

A scratch proof of the rotation and depth steps exists in this session's scratchpad (a four-frame axe swing built from characters.png plus tool_icons.png, 14 colours, alpha 0/255). It reads as a swing but is not shippable: the wind-up frame is hidden behind the body and the second frame crosses her face. Treat it as evidence the mechanism works and the per-frame judgement is the real cost, not as a starting sprite.

The first real use is the player's action frame. player/player.gd:885 reuses walk frame 3 as the swing (D-8 tier-(a) budget, 'one frame doing a second job'). A derived swing would replace that stand-in without a generation call.
first_action: Write tools/spritesmith.py with the pivot-rotation and palette-verify operations, and prove them by regenerating bot_mk2.png from bot.png so the checked-in file is reproduced byte for byte
source_message: Filed out of Daniel's 2026-09-08 question about whether to switch from Retro Diffusion to an LLM driving Aseprite. The recommendation was to keep Retro Diffusion and adopt the underlying idea — authoring pixels directly at native resolution in a locked palette — in the derived-frame lane, which is where our pipeline is weakest.
